summary: Explains how inter-domain multicast routing works when sites use the Locator/ID Separation Protocol. It is an experimental specification covering multicast across LISP and non-LISP boundaries.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending one message to a whole group of friends still works when everybody's addresses have been split into a name and a location.

questions: how does multicast work with lisp
what is an s-eid g state
subtitle: How inter-domain multicast keeps working when sites split their addresses into IDs and locators with LISP.

tldr.problem: LISP separates host identity (EIDs) from location (RLOCs), so multicast sources identified by EIDs may not be routable in the core, and multicast trees need to cross LISP and non-LISP sites.
tldr.mechanism: Sites keep (S-EID,G) state, the core keeps (S-RLOC,G) state, and ITRs and ETRs translate between them by encapsulating multicast in multicast and mapping the source address of PIM Join/Prune messages.
tldr.outcome: No packet formats change and no host changes are needed, only a translation at the control plane. The RFC is Experimental and leaves several areas open, such as mPITRs, mtrace and locator reachability.

today: RFC 6831 is an Experimental document published in January 2013, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 6830 and RFC 6832.

sections.title: Multicast Meets Locator/ID Separation
sections.content:
LISP (RFC 6830) creates two namespaces: Endpoint IDs (EIDs) used inside sites and Routing Locators (RLOCs) used by the core. A mapping function turns a site's EID-Prefix into its locators.

For unicast, both source and destination addresses must be mapped. For multicast only the source needs mapping, because a group address is logical and not topology dependent. So this specification focuses on mapping the source EID of a multicast flow while the distribution tree is built and while packets are delivered.

The approach needs no packet format changes and no change to multicast operation inside a site. The RFC sees only operational changes for PIM-ASM, MSDP and PIM-SSM, and does not address BIDIR-PIM in depth. It also lists open work: multicast traffic engineering, multicast proxy-ITRs, mtrace and locator reachability.
sections.plainLanguage: A group chat name does not depend on where anyone lives. Only the sender's home address needs translating, so the rest stays simple.

sections.title: How a Multicast Tree Is Built
sections.content:
The basic model is to encapsulate a multicast packet inside another multicast packet. The ITR copies the inner group address to the outer destination, uses its own RLOC as the outer source, and keeps the host's EID as the inner source.

The sequence goes like this. Receivers join with IGMP, using source EIDs in IGMPv3, as (S-EID,G). The receiver site's ETR looks up S-EID in the mapping database and picks an RLOC using the same priority and weight mechanism as unicast. It then builds two PIM Join/Prune messages: one with (S-EID,G) unicast to the ITR, and one with (S-RLOC,G) so the core builds state to the ITR. When the source sends, the ITR prepends a LISP header and replicates on each interface that joined (S-RLOC,G); core routers replicate where the tree fans out. Each ETR decapsulates and looks up (S-EID,G) to reach its receivers.

The consequence is a distribution tree stored in three parts: (S-EID,G) in the source site, (S-RLOC,G) in the core, and (S-EID,G) in each receiver site. The cost is that many S-EIDs can map to one S-RLOC, so data may reach sites that did not join that exact source. Giving an ITR several RLOCs reduces this.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender puts the message in a bigger envelope with the router's own address on it. The envelope travels to everyone in the group, and each receiving router opens it and hands out the message inside.

sections.title: Protocol Changes and Forwarding Rules
sections.content:
IGMP and MLD need no changes, since they are link-local and group addresses need no translation. MBGP and MSDP need no changes either, but MBGP advertises RLOC-space prefixes, and MSDP RP addresses must be mapped into a routable address for peer-RPF checks across sites. PIM-SSM needs a small change: Join/Prune messages carry EID addresses inside a site and must be converted to RLOC addresses when crossing the site boundary. PIM-ASM needs no special action for shared-tree joins, and there is no (*,G) state in the core. For BIDIR-PIM the RFC recommends statically configured RPs.

On the data plane, encapsulation is simple because no EID-to-RLOC lookup occurs during forwarding. An ETR strips the outer header and looks up (S-EID,G); there is no Data-Probe logic as in unicast. If no matching (S-EID,G) state exists for the inner header, the packet is discarded.

If an ITR becomes unreachable, ETRs joined to it must trigger new Join/Prune messages to a new ITR, which is more disruptive than a normal RPF change. Using anycast addressing for ITRs can reduce this.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost nothing has to change. Routers just rewrite the sender's name into a home address when a request crosses from one neighborhood to another.

sections.title: Working with Non-LISP Sites and Address Families
sections.content:
Sites come in three kinds: non-LISP, uLISP (LISP for unicast only), and LISP-Multicast. A uLISP site is treated as non-LISP for multicast. An ETR can tell the difference through the multicast priority in the mapping database: when Mpriority is set to 255, the site is not multicast capable.

For a LISP source with non-LISP receivers there are two answers. One is LISP-NAT with a routable source address, so the ITR forwards like an ordinary router. The other is a multicast proxy-ETR (mPETR), which advertises a coarse EID-Prefix, draws the (S-EID,G) joins, and decapsulates for the receivers. For a non-LISP source, multicast proxy-ITRs (mPITRs) are under study and described as work in progress.

For a LISP source with mixed receivers, the options are to send two packets (one encapsulated, one native) or to always encapsulate and rely on mPETRs. The RFC concludes that uPITRs for unicast and mPETRs for multicast look like the sweet spot.

On address families, the RFC counts 502 combinations of site types and families. It therefore requires that each tree is either IPv4 or IPv6, that ITRs encapsulate only with inner and outer headers of the same family, and that only locators of the same family MUST share the best multicast priority.
sections.plainLanguage: Some neighborhoods use the new address system and some do not. A helper at the border translates, so everyone in the group still gets the message.

sections.title: Embedded RPs, Mtrace and Security
sections.content:
With IPv6 Embedded-RP group addresses (RFC 3956), end-site routers treat the embedded RP as an EID, but core routers need an RLOC. So the receiver site's ETR maps the group address to one with an RLOC-space RP and sends a unicast (*,G) Join/Prune to the ITR. If core routers support RPF Vectors (RFC 5496), EID data could pass through the core, but that works only in a small set of cases and is not recommended because of slow convergence. Mtrace MUST be consistent with unicast traceroute, with the design to be determined, building on mtrace version 2.

Security concerns are mostly those of base LISP and multicast generally. One specific risk is that when several S-EIDs map to the same (RLOC,G) core tree, a malicious receiver site joining a different (S-EID2,G) can cause legitimate sites to receive data from S-EID2 that they did not ask for. The authors say no other differences are known but the topic has not been investigated deeply.
sections.plainLanguage: If two senders share one delivery truck, a sneaky listener could ask for the second sender and everyone on the truck would get those messages too.
